open_obligations: Note that LLM judges stand in for humans, so the second half of Leike et al.'s question is not directly tested.
Check whether the debaters are much stronger than the judges on each closed task.
Check whether the mixed result is driven by task-specific factors such as GSM8KQA arithmetic.
in.other_title: Closed QA without information asymmetry: debate vs direct QA depends on judge strength
in.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether debate's central assumption holds outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements and whether humans can accurately judge a debate when the debaters have superior persuasion and deception ability. On closed tasks (MMLU, GSM8KQA, PrOntoQA, TruthfulQA, GPQA) without information asymmetry, Kenton et al. report debate beats consultancy but versus direct QA only GPT-3.5 benefits (p = 0.037), for Pro 1.0 the difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.1), and Gemma7B and Pro 1.5 do worse; judges are LLMs, not humans.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate helps weaker judges on questions without verifiable evidence, for closed QA tasks with LLM judges and Gemini Pro 1.5 debaters

open_obligations: Check whether the quote verification tool, which marks quotes that directly match the text as verified, puts Khan et al.'s QuALITY debates inside the easily fact-checkable domains Leike et al. set aside.
Check whether the correct-answer advantage survives without the quote verification tool.
Compare with Kenton et al., who do not find the advantage growing with Elo.

Note that Khan et al.'s debaters are LLMs using best-of-N or critique-and-refinement, with persuasiveness measured as Elo; the cited passages do not show them trained to converge to a Nash equilibrium, as Leike et al. say the debate agent needs to be.
in.other_title: Arguing the correct answer is easier, and the advantage grows with debater persuasiveness
in.rationale: Both records concern debate's central assumption that it is easier for the agent to tell the truth than to lie. Leike et al. ask whether it holds outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements. Khan et al. report debaters get higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that this advantage grows with aggregate Elo, suggesting that, for debates in QuALITY, telling the truth is easier than lying. In each of Khan et al.'s protocols, expert models present quotes from the text through a tool that marks a quote as verified when it directly matches a portion of the text, and the judge is instructed to trust only verified quotes; the cited passages do not show that this setting lies outside easily fact-checkable domains, so the two records ask the same question in different settings.
in.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: whether telling the truth is easier than lying in debate, which Leike et al. ask for domains outside easily fact-checkable statements and Khan et al. test for LLM debaters on QuALITY with a quote verification tool and LLM judges

text: Discussing debate, the authors say that initial MNIST experiments, in which debating agents boost the accuracy of a sparse classifier, are promising but more research is needed to determine whether debate is a scalable alignment approach. They pose two questions: does debate's central assumption (that it is easier for the agent to tell the truth than to lie) hold outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements, and can humans accurately judge the debate even if the debaters have superior persuasion and deception ability?
title: Does debate's honesty assumption hold beyond fact-checkable claims; can humans judge?
